                                       PROJECT NO. 58000



 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                             §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                         §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                       §                OF TEXAS
 IN THE ERCOT REGION



        CPS ENERGY’S COMMENTS TO STAFF’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION AND
                          REQUEST FOR COMMENTS


TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

       CPS Energy submits these comments in response to the Staff Proposal for Publication (PFP)

in Project No. 58000. On June 11, 2026, Commission Staff filed a memorandum requesting

stakeholder comments on proposed amendments to §25.192 relating to Transmission Service Rates,

§25.193 relating to Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factors (TCRF), and

§25.252 relating to Large Load Customer Tariffs as well as general comments regarding large load

provisions. A revised PFP was filed by Commission Staff on July 9.

       CPS Energy appreciates the opportunity to comment on these important updates. As a

municipally owned utility (MOU) and transmission service provider (TSP) in ERCOT, CPS Energy

supports regulatory updates that enhance cost causation, fairness, transparency, and administrative

efficiency.

       While CPS Energy supports the overarching goal of aligning transmission cost recovery with

evolving system conditions and legislative directives under Senate Bill 6, several proposed revisions

introduce operational, jurisdictional, and financial implications that warrant clarification or

modification. Our comments below correspond to the structure of the proposed rules.
                                        I. General Comments

Wholesale Transmission Service at Distribution Voltage (WTS-DV)

   CPS Energy is opposed to the implied expansion of Commission jurisdiction suggested in

§25.192(c)(2) related to WTS-DV.            Embedding WTS-DV requirements within §25.192

(Transmission Service Rates) risks conflating distribution and transmission cost recovery and will

expand Commission jurisdiction into MOU distribution ratemaking. See CPS Energy’s separately

filed comments related to this provision.

Support for 12CP

CPS Energy supports replacing the 4CP methodology with a monthly 12CP structure that better

aligns costs with year-round system usage.

                                       II. Section-Specific Comments

§25.192(b)(6) – Definition of Large Load Customer

       The proposed language for this section defines a large load customer as “an entity that is

subject to §25.194 of this title.” According to §25.194(c)(9), a large load customer is defined as

“[a]n entity requesting a new or expanded interconnection where the customer’s total expected

non-coincident peak demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75 MW.” CPS Energy

recommends broadening the definition of large load customer to encompass all customers with

loads equal to or exceeding 75 MW rather than limiting to large loads requesting “a new or

expanded interconnection.” Applying the minimum billing demand to all large load customers

will help ensure that residential and small commercial customers do not bear a disproportionate

share of transmission costs. Additionally, in accordance with rate-setting principles, all similar

customers should be treated equally.
 §25.192(d)(1) – 12CP Load Value for TSP Rate Calculation

       The proposed language in this section directs TSPs to use the “most recently approved

ERCOT 12CP load in effect prior to the date of approval of the TSP’s new network transmission

service rate in the proceeding.” CPS Energy respectfully recommends removing the following

provision:

       “The rate approved may not exceed the noticed rate under any circumstances.”

If 12CP values decline year over year, this rule may offer conflicting instructions to TSPs;

therefore, it should be eliminated.

§25.192(e)(1)(C) – Offsetting Reductions to Transmission Cost of Service

       CPS Energy requests that the Commission include in this section the non-refundable

interconnection fee as an offsetting reduction to transmission cost of service. Please see suggested

language below. This will help ensure uniform reporting practices across all Transmission Service

Providers (TSPs) and is consistent with provisions of §25.192(k).

       (C)     the offsetting reduction to transmission cost of service for any network export rate

               revenues as described in subsection (g)(2) of this section and transmission-level

               customer interconnection fees per subsections (e)(6) and (k)(1).

§25.192(e)(6) – Exclusion of Interconnection Costs

       The proposed exclusion of “transmission interconnection costs associated with

interconnection agreements signed after the effective date” should be aligned with the

implementation schedule in Docket No. 58481 governing large load financial obligations.

Misalignment risks creating unrecoverable cost gaps for projects already in development or

partially executed.

       Additionally, CPS Energy recommends replacing the term “transmission interconnect
 costs” with “transmission customer interconnect costs, excluding generation interconnects” to

prevent misinterpretation.

§25.192(e)(8)(B)(i) – Baseline Values

       CPS Energy proposes to remove this section, as adequate transition requirements are

included in §25.192(l).

§25.192(f)(1) –Modification to 12CP Values

       Current proposed language gives the Commission the authority to “approve changes to

DSP 12CP values and the ERCOT 12CP value at any time.” CPS Energy respectfully recommends

that the Commission's ability to alter 12CP values should be restricted once annual billing units

and the transmission payment matrix have received Commission approval.

§25.192(f)(1)(A) – ERCOT Access to Settlement Quality Meter Data

   CPS Energy requests clarification on:

      timing and frequency of required data submissions,

      acceptable file formats and protocols,

      meter redundancy needs,

      cybersecurity requirements,

      whether ERCOT will provide Point Identification (PI) tags for telemetry data points to

       aid in real-time monitoring of large load customers, and

      how this obligation interacts with municipal confidentiality statutes.

       These considerations are critical to avoiding unnecessary compliance risks. CPS Energy

meter data currently accessible by ERCOT requires one-time and ongoing expenses for labor and

materials. Until further data requirements are provided, it is difficult to determine the cost to Non-

IOUs to provide ERCOT access to settlement quality meter data for large load customers.
 §25.192(f)(1)(B) – Minimum Billing Demand Adjustments

       The rule should specify annualization procedures, treatment of partial-year operation, and

line-loss adjustments when substituting minimum billing demand for measured values. Clear

guidance is essential to ensure uniform ERCOT application.

       In addition, current language references §25.193, which is not applicable to Non-IOU

DSPs. If the intention is for minimum billing demand to apply to all DSPs, CPS Energy

recommends relocating large load minimum billing demand provisions from §25.193(d)(2) to

§25.192(f)(1)(B).

§25.192(i) – Commission’s Authority to Require Rate Filings

       Allowing the Commission to require a TSP to file rate revisions “at any time” may create

financial and operational uncertainty.     CPS Energy recommends describing the intended

circumstances for invoking this authority and providing reasonable notice requirements.

§25.192(l) – Transition Requirements

       This section is mislabeled in the PFD as section §25.192(j).

       CPS Energy proposes beginning the initial 12CP period on October 1 following the

effective date of the rule to allow DSPs adequate time to implement technological upgrades and

restructure demand response programs accordingly. Please see below for suggested language.

       (1) Upon implementation of this rule, the first ERCOT 12CP interval will commence on

           the next October 1.      Initial DSP 12CP billing demands, as established under

           subparagraph (f)(1) of this section, shall be calculated based on the twelve-month

           period ending the subsequent September.

§25.192(l)(2) – Compliance Filing to Update Tariff

       TSPs are required to submit a compliance filing to update tariffs within 30 days of adoption
 of this section in the proposed language.       CPS Energy suggests the following revision to

§25.192(l)(2) to streamline the transition process:

       (2) Upon publication of the initial DSP 12CP billing demands pursuant to §25.192(l)(1),

       each TSP shall submit a compliance filing to update its tariff within 30 days. The updated

       tariff must replace any references to 4CP billing demand with 12CP billing demand,

       including the relevant months. Network transmission service rates shall be calculated in

       accordance with §25.192(d)(1). No other modifications should be included.

                                     III. Responses to Questions

1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions

   be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or

   different non coincident (NCP) demands?

       Transmission planning and investment are driven by the contracted peak demand for each

   customer. As a result, minimum billing demand for large load customers should be based on

   the greater of contracted peak demand or actual peak demand for each customer.


2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:


       a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;

       b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or

       c. extended to a longer time period?


       While CPS Energy acknowledges that new rules are being proposed that will require large

   load customers to fund a portion of upgrade costs associated with their interconnection, there

   will still be ongoing costs for operation and maintenance of the transmission grid that large

   load customers will continue to use for years to come. The minimum billing demand ensures
    that large load customers will not be able to avoid these costs and therefore a disproportionate

   share of these costs being allocated to residential and small commercial customers.

      Further, transmission investment is not immediately recovered, as debt service and

   maintenance costs are incurred over many years. Some customers also have lengthy load

   ramps. Large loads must be required to pay for transmission much longer than the construction

   phase to ensure their costs are not shifted to other customers within ERCOT. CPS Energy

   recommends maintaining a fixed 20-year minimum billing demand, with reevaluation at the

   end of that term to determine whether this provision should be retained or removed from the

   standards.

      CPS Energy requests that the commission address the treatment of large load customers

   that enter bankruptcy, leave the location, or transfer ownership to a new entity prior to the end

   of the fixed 20-year minimum billing demand period.


3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand

   lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large

   load minimum billing demand:


    a. reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand

        is some percentage of the customer' s contracted peak demand or maximum

        NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline

        in phases over the years, and how?


    b. be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the large

        load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load

        customer's contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
         year and the large load customer's 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage

        weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases

        over the years, and how?

      Transmission planning and investment are driven by the contracted peak demand for the

   customer. As a result, CPS Energy believes minimum billing demand for large load customers

   should be based on the greater of contracted peak demand or actual peak demand.


4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as

   an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection

   Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power

   electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and

   cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include

   applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large

   computational loads.


      CPS Energy has no comments to this section at this time.


5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include

   transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to

   serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?


      Transmission interconnection costs should be expanded to include transmission

   projects, including system upgrades, identified through batch studies. System upgrades

   required to serve a large load’s full capacity can be significant, and large loads should pay

   either a portion or the full cost of the upgrades needed to support them. However, assigning

   these costs to individual large loads will be challenging because ERCOT will conduct batch
    studies rather than individual studies, making it harder to determine which upgrades

   support which customers.      ERCOT will need to clearly identify which projects are

   associated with each large load and whether those projects benefit a single customer or

   multiple customers. Additionally, clarity is needed on how TSPs should allocate upgrade

   costs when the upgrades also support large load customers of other TSPs or DSPs.


6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of

   whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,

   how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments

   and transmission planning studies?

      Transmission planning performs studies based on customer contracted load. Transmission

   facilities are built based on the contracted load. If a customer is consistently not meeting

   contracted load, transmission capacity should not be reserved for the customer and should be

   reallocated.

      CPS Energy recommends that large loads continue to be reflected based on their Load

   Commissioning Plans (LCPs), or phased energization schedules, rather than their full

   contracted peak demand, as consistently as possible across resource adequacy reporting,

   reliability assessments, and transmission planning studies.         Transmission planning

   assumptions may differ, however, as NERC has an established set of planning assumption

   requirements in its planning criteria.

      This approach reflects the existing process by which prospective customers and TSPs

   coordinate infrastructure development and load interconnection, ensuring that reported

   demand aligns with expected energization and assuring timely capital investments align with

   appropriate market signals. Applying this methodology in a more consistent manner across
    ERCOT reliability planning and resource adequacy reporting processes also improves

   transparency and provides market participants with a more accurate and consistent

   representation of expected load growth and the needs of the system.

                                     IV. Conclusion

       CPS Energy appreciates the Commission’s efforts to modernize transmission cost recovery

rules and supports adoption of final rules that balance cost causation, financial stability, and

administrative practicality.   We respectfully request that the Commission incorporate the

clarifications and revisions outlined above to ensure effective and equitable implementation across

ERCOT.


       Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

                                                             Respectfully submitted,

                                                             CPS ENERGY

 Executive Summary
CPS Energy Comments on Project No. 58000
Rulemaking to Update Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission Cost Recovery in ERCOT

       CPS Energy appreciates the Commission’s commitment to modernizing transmission cost

recovery rules in ERCOT. We support regulatory updates that advance reliability, cost causation,

fairness, transparency, and administrative efficiency.

Summary of Substantive Comments

      Preserve municipal ratemaking authority
          o Remove WTS‑DV language from §25.192, as Commission jurisdiction is limited
             to nondiscrimination review and inclusion risks expanding PUCT oversight into
             MOU distribution rates.

      Apply the 75 MW threshold consistently to all large loads
         o Broaden the definition of “large load customer” so it applies to any customer with
             load ≥75 MW, not just those requesting new or expanded interconnection.

      Align rule implementation with related large‑load rulemaking
          o Ensure §25.192(e)(6) aligns with §25.194 (Docket No. 58481) to avoid
              unrecoverable cost gaps for projects already underway.

      Clarify ERCOT data access requirements
          o Provide direction on timing, file formats, cybersecurity, meter redundancy, PI‑tag
              support, and confidentiality obligations associated with settlement‑quality meter
              data.

      Specify how minimum billing demand substitutes into DSP 12CP values
          o Establish guidance for annualization, partial‑year operation, and line‑loss
              adjustments when replacing measured values with minimum billing demand.

      Limit adjustments to 12CP values
          o Restrict updates to the annual ERCOT wholesale transmission charges; wholesale
              rate calculations shall be based upon the most recently approved ERCOT
              transmission payment matrix.

      Improve transition clarity
         o Begin the initial 12CP period on October 1 following the rule’s effective date to
             allow DSPs time for system upgrades and program adjustments.
         o Require tariff compliance filings only after publication of initial DSP 12CP billing
             demands, limited strictly to replacing 4CP references with 12CP.

 Executive Summary
CPS Energy Comments on Project No. 58000
Rulemaking to Update Wholesale and IOU Retail Transmission Cost Recovery in ERCOT

       CPS Energy appreciates the Commission's commitment to modernizing transmission cost

recovery rules in ERCOT. We support regulatory updates that advance reliability, cost causation,

fairness, transparency, and administrative efficiency.

Summary of Substantive Comments

   •   Preserve municipal ratemaking authority
           o   Remove WTS-DV language from §25.192, as Commission jurisdiction is limited
               to nondiscrimination review and inclusion risks expanding PUCT oversight into
               MOU distribution rates.

   •   Apply the 75 MW threshold consistently to all large loads
           o   Broaden the definition of"large load customef' so it applies to any customer with
               load 275 MW, not just those requesting new or expanded interconnection.

   •   Align rule implementation with related large-load rulemaking
           o   Ensure §25.192(e)(6) aligns with §25.194 (Docket No. 58481) to avoid
               unrecoverable cost gaps for projects already underway.

   •   Clarify ERCOT data access requirements
           o   Provide direction on timing, file formats, cybersecurity, meter redundancy, PI-tag
               support, and confidentiality obligations associated with settlement-quality meter
               data.

   •   Specify how minimum billing demand substitutes into DSP 12CP values
           o   Establish guidance for annualization, partial-year operation, and line-loss
               adjustments when replacing measured values with minimum billing demand.

   •   Limit adjustments to 12CP values
           o   Restrict updates to the annual ERCOT wholesale transmission charges; wholesale
               rate calculations shall be based upon the most recently approved ERCOT
               transmission payment matrix.

   •   Improve transition clarity
           o   Begin the initial 12CP period on October 1 following the rule' s effective date to
               allow DSPs time for system upgrades and program adjustments.
           o   Require tariff compliance filings only after publication of initial DSP 12CP billing
               demands, limited strictly to replacing 4CP references with 12CP.
